jobs.text: On an energy demand forecaster I ran managed training jobs and endpoints inside the client's cloud account, using Hugging Face encoders with AWS SageMaker [E1].

What I can describe is closely adjacent work. For an energy client in 2021, I built a voice-intent classifier using XGBoost gradient boosting tuned with Bayesian search, with chained prompts, tools and output parsers orchestrated through LangChain [E1][E2]. That delivery produced a 15% improvement in the client's key metric [E2]. The operational pattern is the piece most relevant to you. On that project and on a later education engagement delivered in 2025, I built nightly DAGs that retrained and published the model automatically — Airflow scheduling on the education system, which handled text classification over noisy support tickets [E1][E3][E4]. That project showed a 9% improvement in the client's key metric [E3]. If your recommendation engine needs scheduled retraining and a chained LLM layer, that combination is what I've done. The logistics domain itself I'd be learning.

A defect detector for a logistics team needs two things working together: a vision model that holds up on real camera frames, and a retrieval layer that puts the right inspection context in front of whoever reads the output. The closest thing I've shipped is defect detection on factory-line camera frames, deployed on AWS SageMaker, which came out at a 19% improvement in the client's key metric [E4]. The nearest match is manufacturing, where I built a recommendation engine that grounded answers in retrieved passages from a vector index [E6]. On your named stack — FastAPI serving runs through several of these builds [E1][E2][E3], RAG pipelines in [E3] and [E4], SageMaker deployment in [E1] and [E4].

I have no manufacturing client in my delivery record, and I won't describe work I haven't done. My projects have been in education, travel and fintech. The closest match is a churn predictor I built for an education client: reproducible images shipped to their cluster, training jobs and endpoints managed inside their cloud account, and text classification over noisy support tickets [E1]. That engagement was Docker-based, matching your container requirement [E1]. On serving, two travel projects ran through FastAPI — a demand forecaster built on gradient boosting [E4] and a system producing weekly demand predictions with seasonality and holiday effects [E3].

A document Q&A assistant for an education team tends to hinge on two things: retrieval quality over long, structured documents, and being able to reproduce exactly which configuration produced which answer. On retrieval, I built a RAG pipeline for a media client's support operation, where retrieval fed a text classification layer over noisy tickets [E1]. I also built a RAG pipeline on a real estate demand forecasting project delivered in 2025 [E3]. Different domains, but the same underlying pattern of chunking, embedding, retrieval and evaluation carried across both. For tracking, I logged runs in MLflow on the media price optimiser [E1], and in a fintech recommendation engine I logged every experiment's parameters and artefacts to a registry using MLflow [E2]. That isn't a core strength of mine yet.

Your contract summariser needs three things working together: a scheduler, a retrieval index, and a managed training path. That's the order I'd scope it in. I've built a contract summariser repo that uses Pinecone as the managed similarity index and AWS SageMaker for the model work [E3]. On orchestration, I've written nightly Airflow DAGs that retrain and publish a model automatically, delivered in 2025 for a voice-intent classifier [E1][E2]. Pinecone also sat behind a document Q&A assistant, where answers were grounded in retrieved passages from the vector index [E4], and I've run SageMaker training jobs and endpoints inside a client's own cloud account [E5][E6]. My contract summariser work was for a media client [E3], and the other projects were education, real estate and energy [E1][E4][E6]. I'd want a short conversation about your contract types, languages and volume before committing to an approach. The closest pattern to what you're describing is retrieval-grounded summarisation with a scheduled refresh cycle. That's where I'd start.

Your post asks for five specific pieces and a healthcare reference, so let me take them in order. Subscription billing sits at the centre of a retail inventory tracker I delivered: card checkout, webhooks and subscription billing, with Playwright tests and an outcome of 45% improvement in the client's key metric [E6]. OAuth appears in two builds — third-party sign-in with token refresh and scopes in a logistics inventory tracker [E1], and the same sign-in pattern in an education admin dashboard that also used Docker for deployment [E4]. Docker shows up again in a fintech admin dashboard, containerised services started from a single compose file [E3]. A learning portal for an energy team is mostly an access problem: staff sign in, see the modules their role allows, and the interface stays maintainable as courses change. Those are the parts of your post I can point to concrete work on. Django: an education admin dashboard delivered in 2021 ran on a Django backend with server-rendered pages, third-party sign-in using token refresh and scopes, and Docker deployment on AWS [E1][E2]. Tailwind: a real estate client portal delivered in 2024 was styled with Tailwind, with containerised services and Celery workers, and produced a 34% improvement in the client's key metric [E4]. A logistics inventory tracker used a utility-class design system with responsive breakpoints [E5].

A manufacturing client portal usually comes down to two things: letting customers see live order status without refreshing, and keeping slow work like report generation and email off the request path. Redis has been the caching layer on several builds: a fintech order-tracking app with websocket live updates [E1], an energy marketplace storefront with OAuth login [E2], and a retail inventory tracker [E3]. On the retail inventory tracker it ran the task queue behind a GraphQL API [E3], and on a travel admin dashboard Celery handled emails and report generation [E4]. For OAuth I've implemented third-party sign-in with token refresh and scopes [E5], plus OAuth login on the energy marketplace [E2] and on a logistics inventory tracker that pushed order status to open browsers in real time [E6]. That logistics tracker is the closest analogue to what you're describing — inventory data, authenticated users, live status — so the patterns would carry over rather than starting cold.

Your retail client portal combines live updates, payments, and cloud hosting, and I should be direct up front: my portal work has been in real estate and fintech, not retail. The technical overlap is close, though, and here is what I can point to. On AWS, I built and delivered a real estate appointment scheduler hosted on AWS with a load balancer, managed database and CDN, plus a background task queue for emails and report generation [E1][E2]. On WebSockets, both portals I delivered used them for live updates: a real estate client portal built on event-loop based JavaScript services with strictly typed front and back ends [E3], and another portal that added Stripe payments alongside the WebSocket layer [E5]. On Stripe, I integrated payments in that real estate portal [E5] and in a travel marketplace storefront, where I also handled OAuth login and rate limiting in front of the database [E6]. End-to-end browser testing is not a core strength of mine, so I would rather flag that than claim otherwise.

On education specifically: I built an admin dashboard on a Django backend, hosted on AWS with third-party sign-in including token refresh and scopes, deployed via Docker [E3]. The same project's repo shows the batteries-included Python framework with a load balancer, managed database and CDN [E4]. GraphQL I've delivered elsewhere: a manufacturing client portal with a Postgres database and event-loop JavaScript services [E1], and a retail inventory tracker that included card checkout, webhooks and subscription billing [E2] — the billing work there is the closest thing I have to your subscription model. WebSocket live updates I've shipped in a real estate client portal [E5] and a fintech order-tracking app [E6].

A marketplace storefront for a travel team lives or dies on the booking and checkout path, so that is where I would start: the database layer underneath it and end-to-end coverage of the flow a customer actually walks through. On Playwright, I built the browser end-to-end regression suite in CI for a retail inventory tracker, which ran the buying flow on every change [E1], and delivered Playwright tests alongside Celery workers, Redis caching and subscription billing on that project [E2]. For PostgreSQL, I built the database for a retail booking platform with a React UI and Django backend, which produced a 31% improvement in the client's key metric [E3], and used PostgreSQL with Redis caching for a healthcare CRM pushing live order status to open browsers [E4]. My Docker work includes containerised services started with a single compose file [E5] and a Docker deployment for an education admin dashboard [E6]. That dashboard was also hosted on AWS [E6].

I've also shipped on the travel side before: a travel marketplace storefront in 2026 with Stripe payments, OAuth login, Docker deployment and rate limiting in front of the database [E4], and a travel admin dashboard with a relational schema, card checkout and subscription billing, and a Celery task queue handling emails and report generation [E5]. To be precise about that travel experience: both were storefront and internal admin work, not a client-facing portal. My portal builds have been in other industries — a real estate client portal in 2024 using Stripe payments and Celery workers, containerised so services start with one compose file [E3], and a manufacturing portal in 2021 with a GraphQL API and third-party sign-in with token refresh [E6]. Playwright and Celery together covered a retail inventory tracker, where the browser end-to-end regression suite ran in CI alongside Celery workers for emails and report generation [E1], and that project also shipped a GraphQL API with webhooks and subscription billing [E2]. If the portal needs to sit on that same combination of payments, background jobs and tested UI, the pieces are familiar ground.

On the SQL side, I have written window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables [E1], and built BigQuery serverless queries over event logs plus ETL jobs consolidating five source systems [E4]. My dbt work includes a versioned, tested transformation layer over a warehouse [E5]. For reporting, I have delivered Tableau dashboards for client studies [E1][E6], and I run randomised experiment design with significance and power checks rather than eyeballing before-and-after numbers [E1][E3]. Two of those engagements produced a 41% and a 43% improvement in the client's key metric, in media and fintech respectively [E1][E6]. On your question about travel specifically: travel is one of the sectors I have delivered projects in across 22 engagements [E2], but my documented case studies are media and fintech, so I cannot show you a travel pricing analysis I have run before [E1][E6]. If a comparable structure — demand segmentation, tested transformations, dashboard delivery — maps to your data, I can walk through how I would approach it.

Retention work for a travel business usually turns on cohort definition: first-trip month, acquisition channel, destination or trip type, and then measuring repeat bookings against cohort windows rather than calendar months. Getting that definition right is where a cohort study succeeds or fails, so it is where I would start. Your stack is the one I work in. SQL, BigQuery, Python, Excel and Airflow all appear in my toolkit [E4]. I have built serverless BigQuery warehouse queries over event logs, with role-based access and clustering [E1], and run ETL jobs consolidating five source systems including deduplication and repair of inconsistent customer records [E2] — the plumbing any cohort study sits on. For the analysis layer, I have delivered a customer segmentation study using Python automation and Tableau dashboards, with window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables [E3]. On your travel question specifically: travel is one of the industries I have delivered projects in across 22 engagements [E4], but I have no travel-specific case study written up, and I will not describe work I cannot evidence. The closest documented analogue is the media segmentation study [E3]. Excel appears in my skills list [E4]; my project write-ups do not show it in use, so treat that as familiarity rather than a demonstrated strength.

That's the shape of work I've done: a travel finance close model producing monthly revenue projections with backtests, built on window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables [E1]. On pandas, I've handled dataframe wrangling, joins and reshaping in Python, including ETL jobs consolidating five source systems and scripts that replaced a manual weekly reporting routine [E3][E4]. Snowflake sits in my toolkit alongside SQL, dbt and Airflow [E6]. One point I want to be straight about: my project history covers 22 delivered projects across sectors including energy [E6], but I don't have a documented energy close engagement I can point you to, so I won't claim one.

A segmentation study lives or dies on whether the segment tables land reliably, so the pipeline matters as much as the clustering. I've built dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules in Airflow with a versioned, tested transformation layer over a warehouse, using window functions and CTEs against multi-million-row tables [E1]. On a manufacturing reporting build I handled deduplication and correction of inconsistent customer records feeding scheduled refreshes [E3], which is close to the record-quality work a segmentation study needs before any grouping is trustworthy. Two gaps I want to be upfront about. My comparable work is in energy, where I orchestrated an Airflow and dbt KPI suite with statistical analysis and drill-down reporting [E2], and in travel finance, where I built monthly revenue projections with backtests over multi-million-row tables [E4, E1]. That financial modelling is the nearest analogue to segment-level value analysis, and I'd rather say so than stretch the fintech framing.

Your supply-chain brief sits in an unusual place: the analysis has to satisfy a fintech team, which usually means the output feeds revenue projections and close processes rather than an ops dashboard. On Power BI, I built a manufacturing KPI reporting suite that included deduplicating and fixing inconsistent customer records, orchestrated through Airflow [E1]. For a retail warehouse migration I delivered Power BI reports on top of BigQuery with dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules [E2]. On the finance side, I've written DAX measures and scheduled refresh for a finance audience [E4]. I've built monthly revenue projections with backtests over multi-million-row tables using window functions and CTEs, replacing a manual weekly reporting routine [E3], and handled statistical analysis and forecasting in the warehouse migration work [E2]. That project also involved hypothesis tests, confidence intervals and regression diagnostics [E4]. One honest gap: my documented case studies are in manufacturing, retail and travel finance — not fintech, and supply-chain analysis specifically isn't a core strength [E1][E2][E3]. The closest analogue is the retail warehouse work, where forecasting sat over operational warehouse data [E2].

A finance close model depends on the reliability of the underlying records, so the parts of this brief that stand out are reconciliation, deduplication and consistent definitions across reporting layers. On Looker, I built Looker explores within a manufacturing KPI reporting suite delivered in 2021, where the core of the work was deduplicating and fixing inconsistent customer records and orchestrating the pipelines with Airflow [E1]. That engagement produced a 36% improvement in the client's key metric [E1]. On Tableau, I delivered a media customer segmentation study in 2022 using Tableau dashboards, data cleaning, Python automation, and window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables, with a 41% improvement in the client's key metric [E3]. The same work included interactive executive dashboards with drill-downs and scripts that replaced a manual weekly reporting routine [E4]. I should be direct about the fit: logistics is not a core strength. My client work has been in manufacturing [E1], media [E3][E4] and fintech [E2], so I cannot describe a logistics close project I have not done. What I can bring is the record-cleanup and dashboard groundwork that a close model rests on.

Let me be straight about where each comes from. For education clients specifically, I delivered an Education survey analysis in 2022: statistical analysis including hypothesis tests, confidence intervals and regression diagnostics, with Python automation replacing a manual weekly reporting routine [E3][E4]. The data work was dataframe wrangling, joins and reshaping in Python, and the outcome was a 37% improvement in the client's key metric [E4][E3]. On Airflow, my evidence sits in other sectors — a dependency-aware nightly pipeline over a versioned, tested transformation layer for a healthcare survey analysis [E1], and an energy KPI reporting suite orchestrated with Airflow and modelled in dbt, which produced a 19% improvement in the client's key metric [E2]. For data cleaning, I have handled deduplication and fixing inconsistent customer records in a media segmentation study [E5][E6]. Orchestration is the part I've repeated most. Dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules using Airflow appear in a healthcare survey analysis project [E5] and a manufacturing KPI reporting suite [E3], and an energy reporting suite was orchestrated with Airflow [E6]. ETL work runs through that same set of projects [E3][E5]. My warehouse work has been on other cloud warehouses, including the education migration [E1]. For an education team, the pattern that matters is getting inconsistent customer records into a tested, versioned transformation layer before cutover. I've built that layer in other sectors as well [E2][E5]. I'm happy to walk through the education case in detail.
